actions.justification: Mandatory first step per ACG GI bleeding guidelines — assess hemodynamic stability. Patient has HR 95 and BP 110/68, indicating possible early hemodynamic compromise requiring immediate evaluation.
Mandatory per ACG guidelines — hemodynamic assessment must be initiated immediately in GI bleeding to determine resuscitation needs and urgency of endoscopy.
Mandatory — large-bore IV access is required for resuscitation and blood product administration in upper GI bleeding. Patient may need crystalloid bolus and/or packed RBCs pending lab results.
Mandatory per ACG GI bleeding guidelines. CBC needed to assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count to guide transfusion decisions and risk stratification.
Mandatory per ACG GI bleeding guidelines. Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) needed to assess bleeding risk and guide management, especially given NSAID use.
Mandatory per ACG GI bleeding guidelines. Type and crossmatch required immediately to prepare for potential packed RBC transfusion given active GI bleeding and borderline hemodynamics.
BMP is needed to assess renal function (critical given chronic NSAID use, which can cause AKI and worsen bleeding risk) and electrolytes. This completes the diagnostic workup per guidelines.

Patient has borderline hemodynamics (HR 95, BP 110/68, MAP 82) consistent with mild hypovolemia from GI blood loss. IV fluid resuscitation per ACG guidelines should precede endoscopy and support hemodynamic stability.

IV PPI is standard of care for upper GI bleeding, especially NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease. Per ACG guidelines, PPI therapy should be initiated promptly to reduce rebleeding risk and support mucosal healing.

GI consultation is essential for urgent upper endoscopy planning in this patient with melena on chronic NSAIDs despite PPI use. Endoscopy is the diagnostic and therapeutic standard of care for upper GI bleeding.
Type and crossmatch should be confirmed/updated to prepare for potential packed RBC transfusion depending on CBC results, given hemodynamic borderline stability (HR 95, BP 110/68).
Prokinetic (e.g., IV erythromycin or metoclopramide) prior to endoscopy improves gastric visualization by promoting gastric emptying of blood clots, per ACG guidelines for upper GI bleeding workup.

Lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and occult hypoperfusion in this patient with borderline hemodynamics (HR 95, BP 110/68). Elevated lactate would indicate hemodynamic compromise requiring more aggressive resuscitation per ACG guidelines.

Serial CBC monitoring is essential in active GI bleeding to trend hemoglobin levels and guide transfusion decisions (transfuse if Hgb <7 per guidelines). Initial CBC is still pending, so scheduling a repeat ensures continuous monitoring.
Initial CBC is pending at 70 minutes; repeating CBC will help trend hemoglobin and guide transfusion decisions (transfuse if Hgb <7 per ACG guidelines) once results are available.
Patient has melena, HR 95, BP 110/68 suggesting ongoing blood loss; administer packed RBCs if hemoglobin returns below 7 g/dL per ACG GI bleeding transfusion threshold.
Trending lactate will help assess tissue perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation in this patient with signs of hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, borderline hypotension).

Surgical consultation is appropriate for NSAID-associated upper GI bleeding with ongoing melena to ensure surgical backup is available if endoscopic therapy fails or patient deteriorates. This is a standard part of multidisciplinary management of upper GI bleeding.

Octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and can help control upper GI bleeding, particularly useful as adjunctive therapy while awaiting endoscopy. Appropriate in this phase given ongoing melena and hemodynamic borderline stability (HR 95, BP 110/68).

CT abdomen can help identify the bleeding source, rule out perforation or other complications, and guide further management in this patient with NSAID-associated upper GI bleed who has already received initial resuscitation and labs.

Patient has ongoing upper GI bleeding with melena despite PPI therapy and NSAID use. With extensive workup already completed and GI/surgery consulted, angiography can help localize the bleeding source, especially if endoscopy is pending or if bleeding is brisk. This is the only available action in the current phase and is clinically reasonable for further characterization of the bleeding source.
ACG guidelines mandate NSAID discontinuation in NSAID-associated GI bleed despite PPI. This is a HIGH severity requirement and has not been completed yet. Continuing NSAIDs is explicitly forbidden.

Urine output monitoring is a key indicator of end-organ perfusion and volume resuscitation adequacy in upper GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability. Helps guide ongoing fluid and transfusion decisions.

GI consult completed, resuscitation initiated, IV PPI and prokinetic given. Next step per ACG guidelines is urgent upper endoscopy within appropriate timeframe for NSAID-associated upper GI bleed with melena.
